results.title: Rubric Reliability - RCampus
results.content: # Rubric Reliability. Rubric validity and reliability are two important factors in the quality of rubrics and assessments. Reliability describes the level of discrepancy in evaluation results when a rubric is used by multiple assessors – or by the same assessor multiple times – on the same item. The more varied the results, the less reliable a rubric is. A reliable rubric has clear enough descriptors to remove as much bias as possible, reducing the likelihood of varying results by multiple raters. Rubric reliability are caused because the rubric is not evaluated the same way, and that’s generally a result of descriptors being vague, subjective, or unrelated, or lack of any descriptors. So how do you fix rubric descriptors? A rubric without any descriptors is really a Likert scale, even it could look like a rubric. * The best way to detect the cause of rubric reliability issues is by analyzing the results of evaluations. As described above, insufficient descriptors are the main cause of rubric reliability issues. If there are no descriptors, the rubric is not reliable. You can also use some computerized computational methods as well as manual eye-balling methods to measure reliability – after a rubric is used by multiple scorers on the same exact items. To manually detect rubric reliability, have multiple raters evaluate the same body of work. The closer the results the more reliable the rubric is. ## How to improve rubric reliability with iRubric:. A few features of iRubric can help you improve rubric reliability:. 1. iRubric can help you make better rubrics with higher quality descriptors:  Rubric descriptors are the hardest part of rubric development. 2. iRubric Inter Rater Reliability (IRR) reports: iRubric generates IIR reports to indicate which parts of a rubric have reliability issues. 3. iRubric Summary and Detailed reports: iRubric generates easy to understand visualizations of how each evaluation and allows comparison of multiple evaluations to detect (1) reliability issues and (2) issues when raters do not follow rubric descriptors correctly. 4. iRubric Aggregate reports:  Another easy way to identify rubric reliability issues is by using aggregate reports for each item where you can easily detect areas of low and high reliability.

results.title: Differential Item Functioning (DIF): Complete Guide to Test Fairness | Cogn-IQ
results.content: # Differential Item Functioning (DIF). Differential Item Functioning (DIF) occurs when test items perform differently for subgroups of equal ability, potentially indicating test bias. DIF analysis identifies items that unfairly advantage or disadvantage specific demographic groups, ensuring test fairness and validity across diverse populations. Differential Item Functioning (DIF) is a statistical property of test items that occurs when individuals from different groups (such as gender, ethnicity, or language background) with the same underlying ability level have different probabilities of answering an item correctly. DIF provides a framework for identifying and addressing such bias at the item level, distinguishing it from legitimate group differences in the construct being measured. * Understand the distinction between DIF and item bias. * Learn major statistical methods for DIF detection. * Recognize the implications of DIF for test validity and fairness. Uniform DIF occurs when the performance difference between groups remains constant across all ability levels. For example, if an item consistently favors one group by the same amount regardless of ability level, it exhibits uniform DIF. Non-uniform DIF occurs when the performance difference between groups varies across ability levels. This method can detect both uniform and non-uniform DIF through hierarchical model comparison. IRT-based DIF detection compares item parameters across groups, examining differences in difficulty, discrimination, and guessing parameters. This approach addresses the contamination problem where DIF items affect the matching variable, providing more accurate detection especially when multiple items exhibit DIF. When examining DIF across multiple groups simultaneously, methods include generalized Mantel-Haenszel statistics, multiple indicator multiple cause (MIMIC) models, and multi-group IRT approaches. Bundle DIF examines differential functioning at the testlet or subscale level rather than individual items. Bundle DIF can reveal systematic bias patterns that individual item analysis might miss. DIF analysis informs item writing and revision processes. Items flagged for DIF undergo content review to identify potential sources of bias, such as culturally specific references, gendered language, or differential curricular exposure. DIF analysis provides empirical evidence for test fairness, supporting legal defensibility under employment and educational testing guidelines. In international testing programs, DIF analysis identifies items that function differently across countries or languages. A handbook on the theory and methods of differential item functioning (DIF).

results.title: A multilevel mixture IRT model with an application to DIF
results.content: Respondents with similar response patterns can be grouped into a latent class by using mixture item response theory (IRT) models, in which different latent classes are allowed to have their specific set of item parameters such that a latent DIF analysis can be conducted (Cohen and Bolt, 2005;Cho and Cohen, 2010). Mixture random-effect item response theory (IRT) models for ERS are developed in this study to simultaneously identify the mixtures of latent classes from different ERS levels and detect the possible differential functioning items that result from different latent mixtures. In major studies, the applications of mixture IRT models focus on measuring a single latent trait and assume that examinee responses from different subgroups follow a specific Rasch model (Rasch, 1960) with different latent trait distributions and different item parameter sets (e.g., Bolt, Cohen, & Wollack, 2001, 2002 Cho & Cohen, 2010;Cohen & Bolt, 2005;Cohen, Gregg, & Deng, 2005;DeMars & Lau, 2011).
